config.title: Build security test cases for common OWASP attacks

intro.title: Build security test cases for common OWASP attacks
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a set of security test cases to detect common web application vulnerabilities as defined by OWASP, such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting (XSS). You will learn how to use the Node.js testing framework, Mocha, along with assertion libraries like Chai, to write and run these tests. The core programming concept involves creating structured test suites that simulate malicious inputs and verify that your application's defenses work correctly. By the end, you'll understand how to implement automated security checks to protect your Node.js applications from real-world attacks.
intro.usecase: Security test cases for OWASP attacks are essential in real-world applications like e-commerce platforms, banking systems, and healthcare portals where user data protection is critical. Developers implement these tests in authentication forms, payment processing modules, and API endpoints to prevent SQL injection, cross-site scripting (XSS), and broken authentication. For example, when building a user registration form or a dashboard with sensitive data display, security tests ensure input validation and output encoding work correctly. These practices help maintain compliance with security standards and protect against data breaches in production environments.

objectives: Construct a test suite to validate input sanitization against SQL injection attacks
Implement test cases to verify proper session management and prevent session hijacking
Configure test scenarios that detect cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerabilities in user inputs
Apply security headers validation tests to ensure protection against common web attacks
Manipulate authentication test cases to verify resistance against brute force attacks
Initialize test environments to simulate insecure direct object reference (IDOR) scenarios
Integrate security testing into existing Node.js application workflows

steps.hint: Use the require() function to import each module. You'll need four separate require statements.

steps.title: Initialize test data for SQL injection
steps.instruction: Create a constant named 'sqlInjectionTests' that contains an array of test objects. Each object should have 'payload' (malicious SQL string) and 'expectedSafeOutput' (expected safe result) properties.
steps.hint: Define an array with at least two test objects. Use realistic SQL injection payloads like '1' OR '1'='1' for the payload property.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have an array of SQL injection test cases ready for use in security testing.
successCriteria: The 'sqlInjectionTests' constant is defined as an array containing objects with 'payload' and 'expectedSafeOutput' properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started creating the test data, but make sure you have at least two test objects with both 'payload' and 'expectedSafeOutput' properties defined.
steps.feedbackWrong: The test data wasn't created correctly. You need to define a constant named 'sqlInjectionTests' containing an array of test objects with 'payload' and 'expectedSafeOutput' properties.

steps.title: Create SQL injection test function
steps.instruction: Create a function named 'testSQLInjection' that takes a test object as a parameter and returns a boolean indicating whether the input is vulnerable to SQL injection.
steps.hint: Define a function that checks if the test input contains common SQL injection patterns like ' OR '1'='1'.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named 'testSQLInjection' is defined that can evaluate SQL injection test cases.
successCriteria: The 'testSQLInjection' function is created with a parameter and returns a boolean value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a function, but make sure it's named 'testSQLInjection' and returns a boolean.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function is missing or incorrectly defined. Create a function named 'testSQLInjection' that returns a boolean.

steps.title: Initialize test data for XSS attacks
steps.instruction: Initialize an array named 'xssTests' with at least two test objects. Each object should have 'payload' (a malicious XSS string) and 'expected' (the sanitized/safe version).
steps.hint: Create a constant variable called xssTests and assign it an array. Inside, add objects with payload and expected properties. Example payload: '<script>alert("XSS")</script>'
steps.expectedOutcome: An array named xssTests is created with at least two test objects containing malicious XSS payloads and their expected sanitized outputs.
successCriteria: xssTests is declared as a const array with at least two objects, each having payload and expected properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure xssTests is an array with at least two objects, each containing both payload and expected properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The xssTests array is missing or incomplete. Please create a const array named xssTests with at least two objects, each having payload and expected properties.

steps.title: Create XSS test function
steps.instruction: Create a function named testXSS that takes userInput as a parameter and returns true if the input contains dangerous XSS patterns (like <script> tags) and false otherwise.
steps.hint: Define a function that checks if the input includes common XSS patterns. You can use includes() method to check for script tags.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named testXSS that can detect basic XSS patterns in user input.
successCriteria: The testXSS function is defined with userInput parameter and returns a boolean value based on XSS pattern detection.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function is named testXSS and properly checks for XSS patterns like <script> tags.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function isn't defined correctly. Remember to create a function named testXSS that takes userInput and returns true/false based on XSS pattern detection.

steps.title: Initialize test data for CSRF
steps.instruction: Initialize a constant array named 'csrfTests' with test objects for CSRF token validation scenarios.
steps.hint: Create an array variable using 'const' and assign it an array of objects. Each object should represent a test case with properties like 'description' and 'token'.
steps.expectedOutcome: A 'csrfTests' array is created with test objects for CSRF token validation scenarios.
successCriteria: The 'csrfTests' array is declared with 'const', contains at least one test object, and each object has properties like 'description' and 'token'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started the CSRF test data, but ensure it's a properly formatted array with test objects containing relevant properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The CSRF test data isn't correctly initialized. Make sure to create a 'const' array named 'csrfTests' with test objects.

steps.title: Create CSRF test function
steps.instruction: Create a function named testCSRF that takes a token parameter and returns true if the token is valid (non-empty string), false otherwise.
steps.hint: Define a function that checks if the provided token is a non-empty string. Return true for valid tokens, false for invalid ones.
steps.expectedOutcome: A testCSRF function is created that validates CSRF tokens by checking they are non-empty strings.
successCriteria: The testCSRF function is defined, takes a token parameter, and returns a boolean based on token validity.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a function, but make sure it properly validates the token (check for non-empty string) and returns true/false.
steps.feedbackWrong: The CSRF test function is missing or doesn't validate tokens correctly. Create a function named testCSRF that checks if tokens are non-empty strings.

steps.title: Create test runner function
steps.instruction: Create a function named runSecurityTests that will execute all your security test functions and log the results.
steps.hint: Define a function that calls testSQLInjection, testXSS, and testCSRF with appropriate test data, then logs the results.
steps.expectedOutcome: A runSecurityTests function is defined that will execute all security tests when called.
successCriteria: The runSecurityTests function exists and contains calls to testSQLInjection, testXSS, and testCSRF functions.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a function, but make sure it calls all three test functions (testSQLInjection, testXSS, and testCSRF).

steps.title: Execute and display test results
steps.instruction: Call the test runner function and log the security test results to the console.
steps.hint: Use console.log() to output the results returned by your test runner function.
steps.expectedOutcome: The security test results should be displayed in the console when the code is executed.
successCriteria: The test runner function is called and its results are logged to the console.
